newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Planned curbs on Russia religion vex rights groups.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Planned curbs on Russia religion vex rights groups.

text.p: Religion, branded the "opium of the people" by Karl Marx and despised by Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin, has made a strong comeback in Russia since the collapse of atheistic communism six years ago.
But although all religions are equal under the country's post-Soviet constitution some, in the eyes of many Russian churchmen and politicians, are more equal than others.

Their backing of a bill that would clamp down on "non-traditional" religious groups and foreign missionaries has sparked fears among human rights activists that Russia is returning to Soviet-style repression and discrimination.

The bill has the blessing of Russia's most senior clergyman, Patriarch Alexiy, and has already cleared its last hurdle in the State Duma lower house of parliament, which is dominated by communists and ultra-nationalists.
It must now be approved by the upper house, the Federation Council, and by President Boris Yeltsin before it becomes law.
PLANNED LAW PENALISES RELIGIONS NEW TO RUSSIA
"There should be order in the religious sphere and this new law will help bring order," Patriarch Alexiy, head of the powerful Orthodox Church, told reporters recently.

The bill distinguishes between "religious organisations", which encompass traditional Russian faiths like Orthodoxy, Islam, Buddhism and Judaism, and "religious groups" that would have to wait 15 years before applying for full legal rights.
In the meantime the "groups" would not have the right to publish religious materials or to worship in public places.

Under the bill, only confessions that were officially registered at least 15 years ago can qualify as "religious organisations", but critics point out that in 1982 Russia was still tightly controlled by the atheistic Communist Party.
The bill "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations" also states that foreign missionaries can only operate if invited by a Russian religious organisation.

"This is a giant step backwards for religious freedom and for civil rights in a law-governed state," said Lawrence Uzzell, Moscow representative of the British-based Keston Institute, which monitors religious rights in central and eastern Europe.
"The bill is also unconstitutional because it denies equal status to different religious organisations," he told Reuters.
ORTHODOX CHURCH ALARMED BY RISE OF EXOTIC CULTS
Supporters of the bill say it will help control the big post-communist explosion in religious sects that have fed on Russians' poverty, spiritual hunger or simple curiosity.
Japan's notorious Aum Shinri Kyo, for example, had many followers in Russia.
"New sects are harmful because they don't consolidate society but divide it. They are often forbidden in their home countries," Archbishop Sergei, chancellor of the Moscow Patriarchy, told Reuters.
Patriarch Alexiy went even further.

"Today's proselytism, by foreign sects and missionaries...in Russia is something of an eastward expansion and you may perhaps draw parallels with NATO's expansion to the East," he said, referring to another issue that has upset Russian conservatives.
But the Roman Catholic Church -- Eastern Orthodoxy's age-old sparring partner -- and many mainstream Protestant churches also face potential obstacles under the Duma's bill.

"The more extreme cults have passed their peak in Russia. Young people are less drawn to them than in the early 1990s. This bill actually enables the state and (Orthodox) church to crack down on the Protestant and Catholic churches and on rivals within their own structure," said Uzzell.
DEEP-SEATED SUSPICION OF VATICAN
The Orthodox Church has long resented incursions by foreign-based churches on to what it sees as its own turf.

"Russia is an Orthodox country. It is not just a word or an interpretation, it is a deep historical truth," said Archbishop Sergei, adding that Roman Catholic expansion into Russia was linked in the nation's collective subconscious to the country's Time of Troubles in the 17th century and to foreign domination.
"The Catholics are establishing missions in Siberia, and at at time when we are talking about unity between the churches this can only divide," he said.

Underlining the deep-seated suspicion between Russia's Orthodox Church and the Vatican, Patriarch Alexiy and Pope John Paul put off a meeting in Austria last month that would have been the first since the Great Schism of 1054.

"Clearly the Orthodox Church is closely tied up with Russian national identity and it has been feeling rather threatened by the influx of often wealthy missionaries from the United States," said Diederik Lohman of Humans Rights Watch/Helsinki.
"But the proposed legislation is not the solution," he said. "It is vaguely worded and so lends itself to arbitrary interpretation."
RELIGION AT BUREAUCRATS' MERCY -- SOVIET STYLE
Echoing this fear, the Keston Institute's Uzzell said a zealous bureaucrat in provincial Russia could use the law to shut down a local parish church.
"It may be used to freeze Catholic or Protestant parishes at current levels," he said.
The liberal daily Sevodnya has decried what it calls a cosy alliance of state, church and parliament.
"The fight against heresy has united the government and the Duma," it said recently, noting the reformist cabinet and more conservative deputies rarely agreed on much else.
Human rights activists said they had been generally dismayed by the lack of liberal opposition to the bill in parliament, where only eight deputies voted against its final reading.
"This partly reflects the more nationalistic mood among Russian politicians," said Lohman.

In recent years politicians of every hue -- including Yeltsin, Communist chief Gennady Zyuganov and ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky -- have played up their links with the Orthodox Church as proof of their patriotic credentials.

"Now we must see whether Yeltsin will sign the bill," said Uzzell. "It could still go either way. Despite his liberal record he still faces two major sources of domestic pressure -- the Orthodox Church and the Russian Communist Party."
